IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.                 OF 2026
@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.13680 OF 2026 
K. SANTHANAM                                                               ....APPELLANT (S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF TAMIL NADU                                      …RESPONDENT (S)
O R D E R
1. Heard. Leave granted.
2. This  Petition  is  directed  against  the  common  Order  of  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Madras dated 04.06.2026 passed in Criminal R.C. Nos.278 & 280
of 2021. In 1987, S.A Rajasekar (Accused No.1) obtained Court permission to
sell his minor’s son’s property and Rs.5,00,000/- sale proceeds were deposited in
a Fixed Deposit in Andhra Bank, Tiruchirappalli under the supervision of the
District Court, Salem. It is alleged that A-1 conspired with Appellant (Accused
No.2), an Advocate practising in Salem to fabricate a letter falsely purporting it
to be of the District Court Order directing release of the Fixed Deposit. On the
1

--- Page 235 ---
basis of the forged letter received from the Appellant, A-1 had delivered it to the
Branch Manager, Annamalai (Accused No.3) through bank clerk PW-6 (Ramesh)
and the said A-3 released Rs.5,00,000/- to A-1 on 01.08.1991. However, this fact
surfaced in 1994, when bank’s reply to a routine Court reminder revealed the
deposit had already been paid out on the strength of an order passed by the
District Court which had never been passed. Hence, noticing the fraud, the then
Principal  District  Judge  lodged  a  Complaint  on  23.05.1994,  leading  to  a
Registration of FIR No.2 of 1994 against three accused persons including the
Appellant herein for the offences punishable under Sections 406, 409, 420, 468,
471 r/w 120-B IPC. On account of A-1 having absconded, his case was split up
and same is pending for trial in CC No.260 of 2010. The Judicial Magistrate No.
IV Salem convicted the Appellant under Sections 467, 471, 120-B r/w 420, 120-
B r/w 468 and 120-B r/w 409 IPC and sentenced him to 2 years Rigorous
Imprisonment on each count and ordered the sentences should run concurrently
with a total fine of Rs.2,500/-.
3. The first appeal in Criminal Appeal No.58 of 2017 was dismissed by the II
Additional  District  &  Sessions  Judge,  Salem  on  31.03.2021.  Criminal  R.C.
No.280 of 2021, filed before the Madras High Court which was heard along with
Annamalai’s (A-3) Criminal R.C. No. 278 of 2021 also came to be disposed of
by a common Order dated 04.06.2026, namely the impugned order. The High
Court confirmed the conviction and reduced the sentence to 6 months R.I. on
2

--- Page 236 ---
each count in view of the Appellant’s age and expressly noting that the real
beneficiary A-1 was absconding.
4. We have heard the learned Advocates appearing for the parties and perused the
records. The findings recorded by the Courts below would clearly indicate that
purported letter Exhibit P-16 did not find a corresponding entry in the outward
register. However, the Appellate Court independently reassessed the evidence
and found that only Appellant would know how it was fabricated and as such
held the prosecution had proved the case beyond reasonable doubt. The said
findings recorded by the Trial Court as affirmed by the Appellate Court was not
rightly interfered by the High Court under the impugned order. We notice that
the findings recorded by the Courts below is on proper appreciation of evidence
which would not warrant our interference.
5. The  Trial  Court  though  had  sentenced  the  Appellant-Accused  for  2  years
Rigorous Imprisonment, the High Court reduced the sentence to 6 months R.I. on
each count and ordered the said sentences to run concurrently, after taking into
account, the Appellant’s age and the delay that had occasioned. The High Court
also noticed that the real beneficiary was the absconding A-1. Having regard to
the age of the Appellant being around 80 years and the medical condition and
there being no antecedent attributable to the Appellant and the incident had
occurred in the year 1991, we deem it proper to reduce the sentence to the period
already  undergone  and  this  would  suffice  and  meet  the  ends  of  justice.
3

--- Page 237 ---
Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed in part. Pending applications, if any,
stands consigned to records.

O R D E R 
1.   Leave granted.
2. By the impugned judgment and order dated 9th April, 2026, the
High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior has rejected the
appellant’s prayer for bail in anticipation of arrest.  
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 0685 dated 17 th
December, 2025 registered with Police Station Kotwali, Ashok Nagar.
It is alleged in the FIR that the appellant has committed offences
punishable under Sections 108, 318(4), 296(b) and 3(5) of the
Bhartiya Nyay Sanhita (BNS), 2023.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant as
well as the respondent.
5. It is not in dispute that the appellant, in terms of an earlier

--- Page 244 ---
2
order dated 4th June, 2026, has appeared before the investigating
officer on 4th July, 2026.
6. It is submitted that Alok Jain and Manoj Lodha, co-accused,
have been granted anticipatory bail; hence, parity is claimed. 
7. In such view of the matter, we are of the opinion that custodial
interrogation of the appellant is not necessary and that there is
sufficient ground for the appellant to be admitted to an order for
grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
8. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set
aside.
9. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
10. It is made clear that in the event the appellant breaches any of
the terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
11. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not, directly or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
12. Also, since the investigation is yet to conclude, we direct that
if the investigating officer calls upon the appellant to join the

--- Page 245 ---
3
investigation, he shall do so by attending the police station.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
15.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2025
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 5954/2026)
BALDEV SINGH ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
CBI ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted. 
2. The appellant, Baldev Singh, was convicted by the learned
Special Judge, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi, under Sections 7 and
13(2)  read  with  Section  13(1)(d)  of  the  Prevention  of
Corruption Act, 1988 1,  and was sentenced to two and a half
years imprisonment with fine of 10,000/- (Rupees ten thousand₹
only) in relation to his conviction under Section 7 of the
P.C. Act and to imprisonment for a period of one and a half
years coupled with fine of 5,000/- (Rupees five thousand₹
only) for his conviction under Section 13(2) read with Section
13(1)(d) of the P.C. Act. Default sentences for non-payment of
fine were also indicated. 
3. Aggrieved thereby, the appellant, Baldev Singh, filed Criminal
Appeal No. 567/2001 before the High Court of Delhi. By
judgment dated 28.01.2026 passed therein, a learned Judge of
the High Court dismissed his appeal. Aggrieved thereby, the
1 For short ‘PC Act’
1

--- Page 252 ---
appellant is before this Court. 
4. We are informed that the age of the appellant, Baldev Singh,
as on date, is over 70 years. The incident, in relation to
which he was convicted of the aforestated offences, dates back
to 08.11.1995. 
5. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and upon
perusing the record, we find that sufficient incriminating
circumstances were clearly made out to support the conclusion
drawn by the trial court against the appellant that he was
guilty of the offences charged. 
6. We are conscious of the fact that the appellant, Baldev Singh,
suffered incarceration as an under-trial only for a period of
five days in November, 1995, but he has been in prison since
13.02.2026, after the dismissal of his appeal by the High
Court. 
7. Given  the  length  of  time  that  has  elapsed  since  his
conviction, it would be a travesty of justice to sustain the
long sentence of imprisonment that he would have to the suffer
at this stage owing to the dismissal of his appeal by the High
Court. 
8. We may note that the minimum sentence prescribed for an
offence under Section 7 of the P.C. Act, as applicable at the
relevant time, entailed imprisonment for not less than six
months. Similarly, the minimum sentence of imprisonment for an
offence under Section 13(2) of the P.C. Act, at that time, was
one year. 
2

--- Page 253 ---
9. As already noted, the appellant was incarcerated on 13.02.2026
and has been in prison since then. He has, therefore, suffered
over 9 months of incarceration in all. Given the length of
time that has passed and his advanced age, we deem it
sufficient  in  the  interest  of  justice  to  exercise  our
jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution and reduce
the sentence of imprisonment visited upon the appellant,
Baldev Singh, to the minimum sentences applicable at the
relevant point of time. 
10. The order of sentence dated 03.08.2001 passed by the learned
Special Judge, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi, confirmed by the High
Court  of  Delhi  by  way  of  the  impugned  judgment  shall,
accordingly, stand modified and the sentences, which are to
run  concurrently,  shall  stand  reduced  to  one  year  of
imprisonment.  The  fine  amounts  shall,  however,  remain
unaltered and, in consequence, the default sentences in that
regard shall also remain unaltered. 
11.The appeal is, accordingly, allowed to the extent indicated
above.  
12.Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

pending proceedings as recorded in Paragraph 7

above, in terms of the settlement;

at Bengaluru]
T.R.SRINATH                                        Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
KARNATAKA STATE AGRO CORN PRODUCTS LIMITED         Respondent(s)
FOR ADMISSION 
WITH
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C)  No.32592/2026 (Item 60)
WITH 
SLP(C) No. 33162-33163/2026 (IV-A) (60.1)
 
Date : 18-09-2026 These petitions were called on for hearing
today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. S N Bhat, Sr. Adv. 
                   Mr. D P Chaturvedi, Adv.
                   Mr. Tarun Kumar Thakur, Adv.
                   Mr. Abhay Choudhary M, Adv.
                   Ms. Anuradha Mutatkar, AOR
                   Mrs. Parvati Bhat, Adv.
                  
For Respondent(s) : 
     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  petitioners  faced  disciplinary  proceedings
resulting in a disciplinary action as well as orders
of  recovery  of  the  alleged  loss  caused  to  the
1

--- Page 284 ---
Corporation from the dues payable to the petitioners.
The  disciplinary  action  as  well  as  the  recovery
direction was challenged by the petitioners through
writ petition.  The petitioners succeeded before the
learned Single Judge against which the Corporation
preferred a writ appeal.  The Writ Appellate Court
found that there was no procedural lapse in the
disciplinary  inquiry;  the  petitioners  were  given
opportunity to defend their cases; and the charges
stood proved.  Based on those findings, the Division
Bench allowed the writ appeals and set aside the
order passed by the learned Single Judge.  However,
the  Division  Bench  clarified  that  the  writ
petitioners would be entitled to payment of earned
leave  in  terms  of  Rule  4.17  (8)  (Note:1(ii)).
Besides, they were also held entitled for gratuity
along with statutory interest. The Division Bench
further  directed  that  those  benefits  shall  be
released within a period of six weeks.  However,
while  closing  the  judgment,  the  Division  Bench
observed -
‘However, the right of the appellant
– corporation to recover the amount
in appropriate civil proceedings is
protected”
2. The petitioners have challenged the order of the
Division Bench on the ground that the learned Single
2

--- Page 285 ---
Judge  had  found  the  charges  to  be  vague  and,
therefore, the Division Bench was not justified in
interfering with the order passed by the learned
Single Judge.
3. Additionally, it was submitted that since there was
no  categorical  finding  in  respect  of  any  loss
deliberately caused by the writ petitioners to the
Corporation, there was no justification to leave it
open for the corporation to recover the disputed
amount through civil proceedings.  
4. We have considered the submissions and have perused
the materials available on record.  Upon perusal of
the record and upon consideration of the submissions,
we notice that the charges,  inter  alia , were in
respect of not maintaining records in a proper manner
and of not ensuring the requisite ratio of supply and
receipt. Those charges are proved in the inquiry and,
therefore,  the  disciplinary  action  taken  by  the
Corporation cannot be faulted.  The view taken by the
learned Single Judge that charges were not specific
is not acceptable having regard to the nature of
charges and the findings returned by the Inquiry
Officer.
5. In  such  circumstances,  the  Division  Bench  was
justified in setting aside the order of the learned
Single Judge. 
3

--- Page 286 ---
6. Moreover, the Division Bench has directed payment of
earned  leave  and  gratuity  along  with  statutory
interest to the writ petitioners, therefore, the writ
petitioners’ grievance that quantum of loss has not
been properly determined to effect recovery from the
writ  petitioners  no  longer  subsist.  In  case  the
Corporation decides to recover any loss, it would
have to initiate appropriate proceeding against the
writ petitioners where the writ petitioners would
have a right to set up their defence. We, therefore,
find no good reason to interfere with the impugned
order(s). However, we deem it appropriate to clarify
that in case the Corporation seeks to recover any
amount of losses by instituting civil proceedings
against the petitioners, the petitioners will have a
right to contest those proceedings on merits.
7. Subject to above clarification, these special leave
petitions stand disposed of.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.
  (KAVITA PAHUJA)                               (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

1. We heard Mr. Kapil Sibal and Mr. Rajiv Shakdhar, the
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
(original plaintiff) and on the other hand, Mr. Gopal
Sankarnarayan, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
respondents (original defendants).
2. This litigation has something to do with the question
whether the ex-parte interim injunction which, at one point
of time was granted to the plaintiff continued or not.
3. In para 51 of the impugned order, the High Court has
observed thus:-
“51. After careful perussal of the Register and
reports of both the Courts below, this Court is of
the firm opinion that there is no existing ad interim
ex parte  injunction order on 15.12.2025, as apparent
on  the  face  of  record,  there  was  no  extension
application on that particular day and there was no
endorsement on the docket as regards extension.”
4. Both, Mr. Kapil Sibal and Mr. Rajiv Shakdhar have many
things to say as regards this finding of fact recorded by
the High Court in para 51, referred to above. Both the
learned senior counsel have many other contentions to raise.
5. We do not propose to get into any further debate on
this.
6. We are informed that the matter is now coming up before
the Commercial Court on 13 th October, 2026. On 13 th October,
2026, the Court is to hear the plaintiff insofar as his
2

--- Page 332 ---
application for injunction is concerned. The other side has
also filed a counter claim and an injunction application.
7. We are of the view that it will be in the fitness of
things if the Commercial Court, without fail hears both the
parties on their respective applications on 13 th October,
2026 and take appropriate decision on the merits of their
respective applications without being influenced in any
manner by any of the observations made so far by the High
Court in the present litigation.
8. Since  we  want  the  Commercial  Court  to  hear  the
applications on 13 th October, 2026, we expect that no time
will be prayed for by either of the parties.
9. With the aforesaid, this petition stands disposed of.
10. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

   Leave granted.
    The High Court, while granting anticipatory bail to
the appellant, directed him to appear before the Trial
Court/Investigating Officer within thirty days from the
date of order and furnish a personal bond of Rs. 25,000/-
in the event of arrest. Owing to ill health, appellant was
unable to appear before the authority. The application
seeking extension of time for compliance of the aforesaid
order, was rejected, vide the impugned order. Aggrieved,
the present appeal has been filed.
We have heard learned counsel for the parties.

time  granted  by  the  High  Court  earlier  shall  stand
extended for a further period of two weeks.
We make it clear that the appellant shall positively
appear before the concerned Investigating Officer on 23 rd
September, 2026 at 11 a.m., and thereafter as and when
required.
Accordingly, the impugned order stands set aside and
the appeal stands allowed.

1. The submission on behalf of the appellant is
that the power to suspend or cancel the registration
of  insolvency  professional  agency  or  information
utility, as the case may be, is to be exercised by
the disciplinary committee upon examination of the
report of the investigating authority and upon being
satisfied that sufficient cause exists for imposition
of penalty as specified in sub-Section (3) of Section
1

--- Page 367 ---
220 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (for
short ‘IBC’). It is submitted that in the instant
case  the  Board  (the  respondent  herein)  did  not
appoint  any  investigating  authority  to  submit  a
report as is required by the provisions of Section
218  of  IBC  rather,  straightway,  a  notice  under
Section 219 was issued which was responded by the
appellant. In absence of an investigation report, the
power under sub-Section (2) of Section 220 to suspend
or cancel the registration of insolvency professional
authority  could  not  have  been  exercised.  The
requirement of an investigation under Section 218
preceding a notice under Section 219 was specifically
raised before National Company Law Appellate Tribunal
(for short ‘NCLAT’) but the same was over-looked
while rejecting the interim protection application. 
2. Our attention has been invited to an order dated

and  operation  of  the  suspension  order  dated
16.06.2026 for a period of ten days. Our attention

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION(S)(CIVIL)  NO(S).  3445/2025
VISHAL DHAR                                   PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
KRITI SINGH                                    RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This petition has been filed by the petitioner-husband
seeking transfer of HMA No.1154/2025 titled as "Kriti Singh vs.
Vishal Dhar”, pending before the Family Court, Gwalior, Madhya
Pradesh to the Family Courts, Pune, Maharashtra.
2. The grounds alleged in the petition is that both the
parties are the residents of Pune, Maharashtra and the petition
has been filed by the respondent-wife in Gwalior. In order to
convince ourselves about the correctness of the statement, we
asked the respondent-wife to produce a certificate stating that
she is permitted to ‘work from home’ at Gwalior, Madhya
Pradesh, since she did not dispute that her employer is at
Pune, Maharashtra. That certificate is not forthcoming. Hence,
we are inclined to believe the version of the petitioner-
husband that parties are residents of Pune, Maharashtra.
3. In view of above, w e, accordingly, allow the Transfer

Application  (IA  NO.199259  OF  2026)  seeking
impleadment of the Ministry of Women and Child Development,
is allowed.
The  said  impleading  applicant  is  arrayed  as
respondent No.5.
Petitioner’s counsel to file amended memo of parties.
Learned Additional Solicitor General appearing for
the fifth respondent submitted that counter affidavit is
being filed in the office today. 
The same shall be taken on record.
We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner in the Writ Petition and the Special Leave
Petition respectively and also learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing for the respondent(s)-Union of India nad
learned counsel for the Bar Council of India.
We have perused the Gender Sensitisation and Sexual
Harassment  of  Women  at  the  Supreme  Court  of  India
(Prevention, Prohitbition and redressal) Regulations, 2013.
These Regulations have been made in respect of the Supreme
Court of India precincts only. 
In  order  to  have  a  wider  coverage  of  these
Regulations insofar as the High Courts and all Courts under
the District Judiciary as well as Tribunals of the Central
and State Governments, other quasi judicial authorities
2

--- Page 383 ---
etc, it is necessary that a separate set of Regulations are
made  as  we  find  that  the  provisions  of  the  Sexual
Harassment  of  the  Women  at  Workplace  (Prevention,
Prohitbition and redressal) Regulations, 2013 cannot be
applied in a straitjacket manner to an aggrieved women, who
belonged to the legal professions practising before other
Courts, Tribunals or other fora.
In the circumstances, we request the learned counsel
appearing for the respective parties to have a joint
consultation so as to draft a set of Regulations applicable
to all the aforesaid judicial and quasi-judicial Courts,
Tribunals and authorities.
Learned counsel for the respondent(s)-Bar Council
also submitted that she would seek instructions in the
matter and endeavour to bring about common Regulation
applicable to all the aggrieved women, who are in legal
profession.
We also request the learned counsel for the Bar
Council of India to ascertain from the Bar Councils of the
States as to whether any extant Regulations are being
implemented in this regard.
List this matter on 25.11.2026.

Court, has at the outset raised an objection that the
Petitioner, which is a Joint Venture (“JV”), is not a
foreign entity, but the JV was constituted in India. He,
thus, submits that the present petition under Section 11(6)
read  with  Section  11(12)(A)  of  the  1996  Act  is  not
maintainable before this Court.
3. Faced with this, learned counsel for the Petitioner

liberty  to  approach  the  jurisdictional  High  Court.

permitted to raise an objection questioning the jurisdiction
of the High Court for appointment of the arbitrator on the
grounds that the constituent(s) of the JV comprise one or
more foreign entities.

as aforesaid.

the non-bailable warrant and Section 82 proclamation. The

shall be considered by the Magistrate and release him on
bail, subject to terms and conditions that the Magistrate
may deem fit to impose. The petitioner shall ensure that he
cooperates with the trial, failing which the Trial Court
would be entitled to cancel the bail.

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Hon’ble Mr. Justice Arun Palli has pronounced a
reportable judgment of the Bench comprising Hon’ble Mr.
Justice K.V. Viswanathan and His Lordship.
1

--- Page 403 ---
2. Leave granted. 
3. The operative portion of the reportable judgment
reads as under: 
“CONCLUSION
47. The  present  case  illustrates  the
distinction at the heart of Order XIV Rule 2.
The  framing  of  all  issues  does  not,  by
itself,  prevent  the  Court  from  directing
prior trial of a qualifying issue under sub-
rule (2). But once the Court has embarked
upon the trial of the issues generally, that
power can no longer be invoked to reorder a
trial already underway. Here, the Plaintiff
had  completed  his  evidence,  and  the
Defendants had entered upon theirs. Issue No.
5 was, therefore, not an issue awaiting a
decision whether it should be ‘tried first’;
it was already part of a composite trial in
progress. Order XIV Rule 2(2) could not be
employed at that stage to convert what was
already  being  tried  together  into  a
preliminary adjudication of one issue alone.
48. Thus,  in  the  wake  of  the  position
sketched  out  above,  the  only  and  the
inevitable conclusion that we could reach is:
that the order passed by the Trial Court, the
judgment of the First Appellate Court as also
the decision rendered by the High Court are
apparently  unsustainable.  Thus,  are
accordingly set aside. The IA No. 2647 of
2018 is dismissed. The suit (OS No. 337 of
2013) is restored to the file of the Munsiff
Court, Kottarakara. The Trial Court shall
accordingly resume the proceedings from the
stage  immediately  before  the  interruption
caused to the ordinary course of trial by
I.A. No. 2647 of 2018.
49. The trajectory of the present litigation
2

--- Page 404 ---
at all forums is a telling illustration of
the very mischief which the procedural law
was designed to prevent. A suit instituted in
2013, with all issues having been framed as
far back as 2015, is being remitted after
over a decade for a decision on merits. Thus,
in the given circumstances we request the
Trial Court to decide the suit within three
months from the receipt of the copy of this
judgment.
50. The  interim  order  dated  08.12.2025
directing a stay of the proceedings in OS No.
337 of 2013 at the Munsiff Court, Kottarakara
stands  vacated.  The  Civil  Appeal  is
accordingly disposed of in the above terms.
No order as to costs. 
51. Needless to assert that this judgment
shall not constitute an expression of opinion
on the merits of the case of either of the
parties. The Trial Court shall decide the
suit on its own merits and in accordance with
law.”
4. The appeal stands disposed of in terms of the signed
reportable judgment. 
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.
 (SHUBHAM SONI)                                  (NIKITA SINGH)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Manish Paliwal, AOR
Mrs. Trupti Das, Adv. 
                   
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and on perusal
of the impugned order, we notice that in execution proceedings, the decree
holder has sought for a decree being executed by invoking Order XXI Rule 32 of
CPC, 1908. The Executing Court on appreciation of facts and documentary
evidence placed before it, has arrived at the right conclusion, which would not
warrant our interference. However, the order of the Executing Court directing
the Judgment-Debtor to be put into civil prison, would require examination, in
the background of the Judgment-Debtor being 81 years old person. Hence, to
that extent the impugned order remains stayed.

--- Page 463 ---
2. However, we hasten to add that the decree that has been passed, which has
reached finality and which requires to be executed in its letter and spirit and
any infraction thereof by the Judgment-Debtor, has been rightly frowned upon
by the Executing court and to ensure that the fruits of the decree is
appropriately enjoyed by the decree holder, this Court would examine either
awarding  additional  compensation  to the decree holder  in  leiu  of  the
compensation already awarded and also examine as to what further directions
can be issued for removal of the encroachment. 
3. With these observations, we issue notice and stay the impugned order only
to the extent of directing the Judgment-Debtor being sent to civil prison and
other portion of the impugned order remains undisturbed.
4. Re list after six weeks.
(RASHI GUPTA)                                   (AVGV RAMU)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

--- Page 657 ---
Notice shall be served by all modes, including dasti. 
We find from the record that respondent No. 2, Rana Pratap
Singh, was denied bail during the pendency of the trial, both by
the Sessions Court as well as by the High Court, on several
occasions, but despite the finding of guilt rendered by the trial
court and his consequential conviction, the High Court deemed it
appropriate to grant him suspension of sentence. 
The reason that weighed with the High Court was the pendency
of several appeals of earlier vintage, which would prevent the High
Court from taking up the hearing of the present appeal for an
indefinite period of time.  As to whether such a reason can be the
ground for suspension of sentence, after a finding of guilt was
rendered against respondent No. 2, displacing the presumption of
innocence that he would have enjoyed during the pendency of trial,
notwithstanding which he was not granted bail throughout, we deem
it appropriate to stay the operation of the impugned order, if not
already given effect to. If respondent No. 2 has not been released
on bail on the strength of the suspension of sentence and the
consequential bail granted by the High Court, by way of the
impugned order, he shall be not be released till the next hearing.

CHANDRABHAN                                        Petitioner(s)

IA No. 272638/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
Date : 21-09-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARAVIND KUMAR
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Abhay Singh, AOR
                   Mrs. Ankita Agarwal, Adv.
                   Mr. Jishnu Adhikari, Adv.                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The issue in the present petition relates to compassionate appointment,
namely, as to when the right to seek such employment would accrue whether
from the date of application or date of death. In the case of N.C. Santhosh Vs.
State of Karnataka & Ors., reported in (2020) 7 SCC 617, it has been held
from the date of application whereas taking note of the other judgments, this
Court in State Bank of India & Ors. Vs. Sheo Shankar Tewari, reported in
(2019) 5 SCC 600  has referred the said issue to a Larger Bench. Hence, we
issue  notice  both  on  the  application  for  delay  as  well  as  on  the  petition,
returnable within four weeks. 
  (NEHA GUPTA)                                   (AVGV RAMU)
